blocks.title: The law suggests...
blocks.body:
In order to use data - often the point of collecting it in the first place - it must be analysed, processed and modified, or even shared with people outside of your organisation. The Data Protection Act 2018 says that data should be used fairly, lawfully, and transparently. It should also be used only for specified purposes, and in a way that is adequate, relevant, and limited to what is absolutely necessary. 

Data usage covers a wide scope of tasks, and brings numerous ethical issues, particularly around transparency, fairness, and bias.

blocks.title: Transparency
blocks.body:
As well as stating an intended purpose up front, organisations should also be ready to clearly communicate how the data is being used. 

Select the arrows to learn more.

items.title: The right to explanation
items.body: It's critical to be able to explain how data is driving a decision-making process and/or how a particular decision was made using the data. Transparency represents a fundamental principle in GDPR: the right to explanation.
items.graphicAlt: icon of a magnifying glass looking at binary code

items.title: Algorithms
items.body:
With an increasing use of algorithms for data-driven automated decision making, transparency has become even more important to help explain how an algorithm arrived at its outcomes. 
This can often be difficult as many algorithms are 'black boxes.' However, methods to help explain their inner workings (explainable AI) are becoming increasingly used.

items.title: Ask yourself
items.body:
• How open are you about data collection, processing, and usage?
  • Are you able to easily articulate and explain how you are using data and for what specific purpose?
  • Are you transparent about how you protect and secure the data collected from consumers?
  • If you're using algorithms and AI, are you using methods to help explain their inner workings and how they arrived at an outcome?

blocks.body:
In terms of fairness - often thought of as 'impartial and just treatment or behaviour without favouritism or discrimination' - the collection and use of data should be proportionate to the challenge or issue it has set out to resolve. The quality of data should also be such that the insights it generates are fair, and that any impact on a particular group can be justified and not be detrimental.

Select each heading from the list below to find out more.

items.title: Value
items.body: Are you offering customers value in exchange for using their data? This is part of what it means to collect data proportionately to the issue it is resolving-that is, improving a product or service your customers use.

items.title: Personal data
items.body: Should you be using personal data at all? Is it fair to do so? You may not need to collect any personal information to achieve your analytics goals.

items.title: Filling the gaps
items.body: Are you collecting data in a fair way, so that all groups are represented? Look for gaps in the data you are collecting - this could lead you to overlook key information you could use to ensure all groups have equitable positive experiences with the product or service you offer.

blocks.title: Bias
blocks.body:
While we acknowledge that humans are often biased and naturally prejudiced, it's a common misconception that machines make cold and objective decisions. The reality is that algorithms can inherit and amplify the same biases present in the data used to build them.

Select the cards to find out more.

items.frontImageAlt: icon of a download arrow into a computer
items.backBody: Because humans decide what data to collect, biases often creep in at the data collection stage-like reporting bias, in which only a fraction of real-world information is captured, so information is underreported for certain groups.

items.frontImageAlt: icon of information moving from a computer to a server
items.backBody: There are a few ways in which bias can creep into data analysis. Data preprocessing can exclude certain groups, and humans can act unconsciously to introduce bias when selecting features for analysis, setting parameters, or interpreting results. Likewise, algorithms may inherit bias from training models.

items.frontImageAlt: icon of information being passed to a person
items.backBody: There are tools and strategies to help minimise bias in data processing and handling. Employing bias detection tools, interpretability tools, and ethical AI frameworks can all help you to increase transparency in how data is handled. Conducting fairness auditing and continually monitoring systems can also help you to stop bias before it causes a negative impact on groups.

blocks.title: Case study: Predictive policing
blocks.body: Due to the mistaken belief that algorithms can provide an impartial and objective solution to crime prevention, law enforcement agencies in several major US cities previously implemented predictive policing programs that used algorithms to allocate resources to 'hot spots' or potential perpetrators - though many of these programs have since been discontinued amid growing evidence that such systems can inherit the biases deeply ingrained in historical crime data. Durham Constabulary in the UK, for example, removed postcode data from its own risk-assessment tool after recognising it could reinforce those biases. When deployed without safeguards like this, the predictions such systems produce can replicate and perpetuate the biases present in their training data.

How can bias be reduced in predictive policing?

Select your answer, then submit.

blocks.title: Case study: Predictive policing

items.text: Regularly updating algorithms to reflect demographic change
items.feedback: Not quite. Updating algorithms to reflect demographic change doesn't address the underlying problem - the bias is baked into the historical crime data itself, and adjusting for demographics alone won't undo that.

items.text: Ensuring transparency in the algorithm development process
Shifting input from largely historical data to largely the judgements of experienced law enforcement officers
items.feedback: Not quite. Relying more on the judgement of experienced officers doesn't remove bias - it just introduces bias from a different source, human rather than algorithmic.

items.text: Ensuring all predictive policing programs in different locations use the same proprietary algorithms
items.feedback: Not quite. Proprietary, closed-source algorithms make it harder, not easier, for stakeholders to scrutinise how decisions are being made - using the same one everywhere doesn't fix that, it just spreads it further.

blocks.feedbackCorrect:
That's right. Transparency is a fundamental principle in ethical algorithm development processes. This means that the methods, data sources, and decision-making processes behind the algorithm used are open to scrutiny and evaluation by external stakeholders, including the public and oversight bodies. 
Updating algorithms to reflect demographic change does not accomplish any ethical goals, as this will not have an impact on the biases inherent in historical crime data. Likewise, implementing further input from experienced law enforcement officers will simply introduce bias from a different source. Implementing algorithms with proprietary code can hinder transparency and accountability, making it more challenging for stakeholders to identify and mitigate bias.
